hints: Look closely at where the poison acts: companion cells in phloem. Remember these cells are packed with mitochondria, so ask yourself what energy-demanding job they do during loading.
Link ATP to proton pumping out of the companion cell, then to sucrose-H+ co-transport in, then to water movement and pressure in the sieve tube.
walkthrough:
**Recall what mitochondria do in companion cells**

Companion cells need lots of ATP for active loading of sucrose into the phloem. Mitochondria make that ATP by aerobic respiration.

Think: poison stops mitochondria, so: $$ATP \ production \ falls$$

**Link ATP to hydrogen ions and sucrose loading**

ATP is used to pump hydrogen ions (H+) out of the companion cell cytoplasm into the cell wall. This creates a steep H+ gradient.

Sucrose then moves back in with H+ by co-transport against its own gradient. No ATP means no H+ pumping, so statement 1 changes, and no sucrose loading, so sucrose builds up in the leaf source cells and statement 2 changes.

**Link loading to mass flow pressure**

In the mass flow hypothesis, high sucrose in the sieve tube lowers water potential, so water enters by osmosis and raises hydrostatic pressure at the source. If loading stops, less sucrose enters, less water enters, and the source pressure falls.

So the hydrostatic pressure gradient between source and sink is reduced, so statement 3 changes. All three change, which is option A.

options.A: All three change. Loss of ATP stops H+ pumping (1), stops sucrose loading so leaf sucrose rises (2), and lowers source hydrostatic pressure so the gradient falls (3).
options.B: This misses 3. Less sucrose loaded means less water entry by osmosis, so hydrostatic pressure at the source must also change.
options.C: This misses 2. If active loading is blocked, sucrose cannot leave the leaf cells normally, so cytoplasmic sucrose concentration in the leaf will rise.
options.D: This misses 1. The H+ gradient depends directly on ATP-driven proton pumps, so stopping mitochondria immediately changes H+ concentration in the companion cell wall.
